title: Supporting breastfeeding and formula feeding
blurb: Support positioning and attachment, assess a feed, advise on expressing and mastitis, and teach safe formula preparation and responsive bottle feeding (NICE NG194).
question: Sophie, 28, is breastfeeding on day 3. Her nipples are sore and pinched after feeds and her baby falls asleep after a few quick sucks. What should the midwife assess first, and how should she offer help?

teach.body: Formally (NICE NG194 1.5.6-1.5.10): professionals should know about milk production, signs of good attachment, effective milk transfer and common problems, and give tailored face-to-face support at every postnatal contact until breastfeeding is established. In plain English: watch a feed, check attachment, explain what you see, and keep supporting her. Ask consent before offering physical help, respect her personal space, culture and preferences, and recognise the emotional impact of breastfeeding.

steps.label: Baby close, in line
steps.sub: head and body straight, facing the breast

steps.label: Nose to nipple
steps.sub: head tips back, mouth opens wide

steps.label: Big mouthful
steps.sub: more areola above the top lip than below

teach.caption: Bring the baby to the breast, not the breast to the baby. Avoid holding the back of the baby's head so they can tip it back.

rows.label: Sucking
values: Quick sucks then rhythmic, audible swallows
Quick sucks only, falls asleep early

rows.label: Nappies
values: At least 6 wet a day after the first days

items: Ask about the parents' concerns, how often and how long feeds are, rhythmic sucking and audible swallowing.
Ask whether the baby is content after feeds and waking for feeds; review weight gain or loss and wet and dirty nappies.
Check the condition of her breasts and nipples.
Observe a feed within the first 24 hours and at least 1 other feed within the first week.
Ongoing concerns: observe more feeds, adjust positioning and attachment, give expressed milk, refer for extra support, assess for tongue-tie.

head: Where
How long
rows: Back of fridge at 4 C or lower
Once the baby has drunk from the bottle
teach.caption: Defrost slowly in the fridge; do not refreeze; never warm in a microwave or on a stove.

teach.body: Mastitis is a swollen, hot, painful area, usually in one breast, sometimes with flu-like symptoms. Advise her to keep breastfeeding as often as the baby wants, check positioning and attachment, hand express if feeding is too painful, use cold compresses, rest, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen. She should not stop breastfeeding suddenly. Redness and swelling persisting over 24 hours despite self-care is an NG194 red flag needing medical advice; if she becomes systemically unwell, think sepsis.

teach.h: Making up a formula feed safely (NHS)

steps.label: Fresh tap water
steps.sub: at least 1 litre; not previously boiled

steps.label: Boil, cool under 30 min
steps.sub: so it stays at least 70 C

steps.label: Cool and test
steps.sub: on inner wrist: warm, not hot

steps.label: Discard leftovers
steps.sub: make feeds one at a time

teach.caption: Water at 70 C or above kills harmful bacteria in powder. Never warm formula in a microwave.

teach.body: First infant formula is the only formula a baby needs in the first year unless there is a medical need. Offer a one-to-one discussion and a practical demonstration of sterilising and preparation. Teach responsive bottle feeding: watch for feeding cues, hold the baby close, pace the feed, recognise signs the baby has had enough (formula-fed babies can be overfed), never prop the bottle, and limit the number of people regularly feeding the baby to support bonding.

Pinched, sore nipples and a baby who falls asleep after quick sucks without moving to deep swallows suggest poor attachment. The midwife asks for consent, then observes a whole feed. She helps Sophie hold the baby close with nose to nipple so the chin leads and the mouth opens wide. She checks for rounded cheeks and audible swallowing, asks about wet and dirty nappies and weight, and arranges to see another feed. If problems continue she considers tongue-tie assessment and expressed milk.

teach.text: Soreness is not a normal price of breastfeeding to be endured: persistent pain usually means poor attachment. And for formula: water must be AT LEAST 70 C (boiled and left no more than 30 minutes), with WATER added BEFORE powder.

items: Ask consent before physical help; observe a feed within 24 hours and another in the first week.
Good attachment: nose to nipple, chin first, wide mouth, more areola above top lip, rounded cheeks, rhythmic swallows.
Expressed milk: up to 8 days at 4 C or lower; 6 months frozen; use within 1 hour once drunk from.
Mastitis: keep feeding, check attachment, cold compress, analgesia; seek advice if over 24 hours despite self-care.
Formula: fresh water boiled and cooled no more than 30 minutes (at least 70 C), water first, pace feeds, no prop feeding.

summary: You can now assess a breastfeed, help with positioning and attachment, and give safe advice on expressing, storing milk and mastitis. You can also teach safe formula preparation and responsive bottle feeding.

A.q: On the postnatal ward, the midwife wants to help Kira, 23, attach her baby. What should she do before touching Kira's breast or baby?
options: Document the feed time first
Call a lactation consultant
Ask Kira for consent
Wait for the next feed
A.why: NG194 1.5.8: those providing breastfeeding support should obtain consent before offering physical assistance with breastfeeding.

whyNot.0: Documentation follows care; it does not replace consent.
whyNot.1: A midwife can support attachment herself; referral is for ongoing concerns.
whyNot.3: Delaying help is not the issue; consent before physical assistance is.

A.q: Which sign suggests a baby is well attached at the breast?
options: More areola visible above the top lip
Cheeks sucked in with each suck of the feed
Quick, shallow sucks all feed long
Nipple flattened after the feed
A.why: NHS: with good attachment you see more of the darker nipple skin above the top lip than below the bottom lip, and the cheeks look full and rounded.

whyNot.1: Sucked-in cheeks suggest poor attachment; cheeks should be full and rounded.
whyNot.2: Effective feeding moves from quick sucks to slower rhythmic swallows.
whyNot.3: A flattened or pinched nipple after a feed suggests poor attachment.

A.q: Under NICE NG194, when should the midwife observe breastfeeds as part of the feeding assessment?
options: Once, just before she is transferred home
At the day 5 visit and at 6 weeks
Daily until the baby has regained birthweight
Within 24 h and once more in the first week
A.why: NG194 1.5.14: observe a feed within the first 24 hours after the birth, and at least 1 other feed within the first week.

whyNot.0: One observed feed before transfer is not the full requirement; another is needed in the first week.
whyNot.1: The first observed feed should be within 24 hours, and 6 weeks is too late for the second.
whyNot.2: NICE sets two observed feeds, not daily observation tied to birthweight.

B.q: Maya, 31, has expressed milk for her baby. Her fridge thermometer reads 4 C. How long can the milk be stored at the back of the fridge?
options: Up to 24 hours
Up to 8 days
Up to 3 days
Up to 6 months
B.why: NHS: breast milk can be stored in the back of the fridge for up to 8 days at 4 C or lower.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is the limit for carrying cooled milk in a cool bag with ice packs.
whyNot.2: 3 days applies if the fridge runs at 5 to 10 C or the temperature is unknown.
whyNot.3: 6 months applies to a freezer at -18 C or lower.

B.q: Tom is making up a formula feed. Which step is correct according to NHS guidance?
options: Use water boiled earlier in the day
Add the powder first, then the water
Cool the boiled water fully to room temperature
Use water left to cool no more than 30 minutes
B.why: NHS: boil fresh tap water and leave it to cool for no more than 30 minutes so it stays at least 70 C, which kills bacteria in the powder. Put the water in the bottle first.

whyNot.0: Water that has been boiled before should not be used; use fresh tap water.
whyNot.1: Water goes in first, then the powder, so the amount is accurate.
whyNot.2: Water cooled to room temperature is below 70 C and will not kill bacteria in the powder.

B.q: Ellie, 26, has a hot, red, painful wedge-shaped area in one breast that started this morning. She feels well otherwise. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Keep feeding, check attachment, use cold compresses
Stop feeding from that breast until it settles down
Express as much extra milk as possible each time
Apply firm massage to the lump to clear the blockage
B.why: NHS mastitis advice: continue to breastfeed when the baby wants, check positioning and attachment, cold compresses, rest and paracetamol or ibuprofen. NG194 1.2.4: seek medical advice if redness and swelling persist over 24 hours despite self-management.

whyNot.1: Stopping feeding on that side allows milk to build up and can worsen mastitis.
whyNot.2: NHS advises not to express more milk than the baby needs.
whyNot.3: Pressure on the breast should be gentle; firm pressure is advised against.

C.q: Lou, 33, plans to formula feed. At a home visit, the midwife sees her prop the bottle on a cushion so she can rest while the baby feeds. What should the midwife advise?
options: This is safe if the baby is on its back
Use an anti-colic teat to make propping safer
Hold the baby close and pace the feed instead
Prop feeding is fine for night feeds
C.why: NG194 1.5.19: discuss the dangers of prop feeding and teach responsive, paced bottle feeding with the baby held close, recognising signs the baby has had enough.

whyNot.0: Prop feeding is dangerous in any position; the parent should hold the baby and bottle.
whyNot.1: A different teat does not remove the dangers of prop feeding.
whyNot.3: Prop feeding carries the same dangers at night.

C.q: Baby Leo, 5 days old, feeds for over an hour at a time, seems hungry soon after, and his mother has cracked nipples despite help with positioning on two occasions. Which additional step does NG194 suggest?
options: Switch to formula to rest the nipples
Assess for tongue-tie
Limit feeds to 10 minutes each side
Introduce a dummy between feeds
C.why: NG194 1.5.15: if there are ongoing concerns, consider observing more feeds, adjusting positioning and attachment, giving expressed milk, referring for extra support, and assessing for tongue-tie.

whyNot.0: Switching to formula is not the NG194 next step; expressed milk can be given if needed.
whyNot.2: Limiting feed length is not responsive feeding and does not address the cause.
whyNot.3: A dummy in the early weeks can lower milk supply and does not address the cause.

C.q: Jade, 29, exclusively formula feeds. She asks whether to buy follow-on formula from 6 months and 'growing up' milk later. What should the midwife say?
options: She should change to follow-on formula from 6 months
Growing-up milk is advised from about 9 months old
Switch to follow-on formula once weaning has started
First infant formula is enough for the first year
C.why: NG194 1.5.17: first infant formula is the only formula milk babies need in the first year of life, unless there are specific medical needs.

whyNot.0: Follow-on formula is not needed; first infant formula is enough for the first year.
whyNot.1: Growing-up milks are not needed in the first year.
whyNot.2: Weaning does not require a change from first infant formula.

reteach.title: Look, listen, ask
reteach.question: Most breastfeeding problems are solved by watching one whole feed carefully. What do you look for, listen for and ask about?

blocks.body: LOOK: baby close and in line, chin touching the breast, wide mouth, rounded cheeks, more areola above the top lip. LISTEN: quick sucks changing to slow rhythmic swallows you can hear. ASK: how do her nipples feel, is the baby content after feeds, how many wet and dirty nappies? If any part is off, adjust attachment and watch again.

blocks.text: A baby who falls asleep before deep swallowing starts may not be attached well. Do not assume he is full: check attachment.

explain.body: Hold the baby close with nose level with the nipple; let the head tip back so the mouth opens wide and the chin touches the breast first. Good signs: more areola above the top lip, full rounded cheeks, quick sucks then rhythmic swallows.

test.q: To encourage a wide gape, where should the baby's nose be as the feed starts?
options: Level with the nipple
Pressed into the breast
Below the areola
Level with her chin
test.why: NHS: hold the baby close with their nose level with the nipple so the head can tip back and the mouth open wide.

whyNot.1: The nose should be clear; the chin, not the nose, touches the breast.
whyNot.2: Starting with the nose below the areola makes the baby tuck the chin and take a shallow latch.
whyNot.3: The baby's position relates to the nipple, not the mother's chin.

explain.body: Ask about feed frequency and length, sucking and swallowing, contentment, waking for feeds, weight, wet and dirty nappies, and breast and nipple condition. After the first few days expect at least 6 wet nappies a day, and stools turning yellow after about day 3.

items.label: wet nappies a day after the first few days
stools change from black to yellow

test.q: On day 5, which finding is reassuring that a breastfed baby is getting enough milk?
options: Black, sticky stools
Two wet nappies in each 24 hours
Six or more wet nappies a day
Sleeping through most feeds
test.why: NHS: after the first few days a baby should have at least 6 wet nappies a day, and stools should become soft and yellow after about day 3.

whyNot.0: Stools should have changed from black meconium by about day 3.
whyNot.1: Two wet nappies a day is fewer than expected by day 5.
whyNot.3: A baby should wake for feeds; sleeping through feeds is a concern (NG194 1.5.14).

explain.body: Hand expression: C-shape with finger and thumb a few centimetres back from the nipple, compress and release rhythmically. Store in sterilised containers: up to 8 days at 4 C or lower, 2 weeks in an ice compartment, 6 months at -18 C. Do not refreeze; do not microwave.
explain.cite: NHS Expressing and storing breast milk

test.q: Baby Ivy drank half a bottle of expressed breast milk 2 hours ago. What should her father do with the rest?
options: Return it to the fridge for later
Warm it in the microwave for the next feed
Freeze it for use within 6 months
Throw it away
test.why: NHS: once the baby has drunk from a bottle of breast milk, use it within 1 hour and throw away anything left over.

whyNot.0: Milk the baby has drunk from should be used within 1 hour, not returned to the fridge.
whyNot.1: Microwaving causes hot spots and is advised against, and this milk is past the 1-hour limit.
whyNot.2: Leftover milk the baby has drunk from should not be frozen; it should be discarded.

explain.body: Use fresh tap water boiled and cooled no more than 30 minutes (at least 70 C); water first, then levelled scoops as the manufacturer says; cool, test on the wrist; make feeds one at a time and discard leftovers. Pace the feed and never prop the bottle.
explain.cite: NHS Making up baby formula; NICE NG194 1.5.19

test.q: Why should formula be made with water at 70 C or above?
options: It dissolves the powder more evenly and fully
It kills harmful bacteria in the powder
It keeps the feed warm for longer
It makes the feed easier to digest
test.why: NHS: powdered formula can contain bacteria even when sealed; water at 70 C or above kills harmful bacteria.

whyNot.0: Even mixing comes from shaking; the temperature rule is about bacteria.
whyNot.2: The feed is cooled before use, so keeping it warm is not the reason.
whyNot.3: Water temperature does not change digestibility.
